name: Profiling and Flame Graphs
intent: Find which functions inside one process burn the CPU, wait on locks or IO, or allocate the memory, by sampling stack traces and merging them into a flame graph.
scenario: After release 412 the GET /orders handler got twice as slow: CPU per request went from 1.0 ms to 2.0 ms. Metrics and traces say the handler is slow but not why. A 60 second profile shows one function, encode_loop inside json_encode, as 58% of all samples because of an accidental O(n^2) loop (work that grows with the square of the input size).
problem: Metrics tell you that a service is slow and distributed traces tell you which service, but neither can say which line of code inside the process is responsible. Guessing and adding timers by hand is slow and changes what you measure. You need a way to attribute time, memory or blocking to functions in a running program with a cost small enough to leave on in production.

howItWorks.title: Sample the stack instead of timing every call
howItWorks.text: A sampling profiler interrupts the process on a timer (perf at 99 Hz, meaning 99 samples per second; async-profiler at 10 ms or every N CPU cycles, pprof at 100 Hz) and records the current call stack (the chain of functions that called each other to reach the running line). It does not need to know when functions start or end. An instrumenting profiler (tracing hooks, sys.setprofile, gprof's mcount) records every call and return: exact call counts and durations, but the hooks cost more than the tiny functions they measure and distort the result, so it is usually kept for debugging, not production.

howItWorks.title: Merge identical stacks into a collapsed list
howItWorks.text: Each sample is a stack such as handler;serialize;json_encode;encode_loop. Samples with the same stack are counted: the collapsed format is one line per distinct stack, 'a;b;c 3510'. Over N samples, the share of a stack estimates the share of time spent there, with a standard error of about sqrt(p(1-p)/N). A function at 3% needs a few thousand samples before its estimate is tight.

howItWorks.title: Draw the merged tree as a flame graph
howItWorks.text: The stacks are merged into a call tree: the root is at the bottom, callees stack on top. Box width is the share of samples that include that frame. The x axis is NOT time: siblings are sorted alphabetically, so left to right means nothing. Self time is the part of a box not covered by its children (the exposed top edge); total (inclusive) time is the whole width. A wide plateau at the top is a function burning time itself; a tall narrow tower is just deep call nesting and costs little.

howItWorks.title: Choose what you sample: CPU, wall clock, allocations
howItWorks.text: A CPU profile only samples threads that are running, so it never shows time spent waiting. A wall-clock (off-CPU) profile also samples blocked threads: time in a mutex, a socket read, a sleep or a disk wait shows up as frames like futex_wait or read. Allocation and heap profiles sample by bytes allocated (every ~512 KiB in Go's pprof, TLAB-based in async-profiler) and show who allocates or who still holds memory. Pick the mode that matches the symptom: high CPU, slow but idle, or growing memory.

howItWorks.title: Compare profiles before and after
howItWorks.text: A differential flame graph subtracts two profiles (normalized to the same total) and colours frames by growth or shrinkage. It answers 'what changed in this release' directly. Run continuous profiling in production (Parca, Pyroscope, Grafana Phlare, Google Cloud Profiler, Datadog) at about 100 Hz per process, which costs roughly 1 to 2 percent CPU, and keep profiles tagged by version so the before and after exist when you need them.

howItWorks.title: Read it with the pitfalls in mind
howItWorks.text: Frames need symbols (function names): stripped binaries and JIT code show addresses until symbolized, and frame-pointer-less builds need DWARF or ORC unwinding. The optimizer inlines small functions, so their time is attributed to the caller unless inline debug info is used. Safepoint-biased JVM profilers only see stacks at safepoints and mislead on tight loops. Too low a rate or too short a window misses small functions, and a rate that locks step with a periodic task aliases.

pros: Points at a function and often a line, which metrics and traces cannot do
Sampling cost is proportional to the rate, not to the number of calls: about 1% CPU at 100 Hz
Works on a running production process with no code changes in most runtimes
Differential profiles show exactly what a release changed
One picture shows the whole distribution of time, so surprises (a 3% logger, a 60% regex) stand out
cons: Statistical: small functions need many samples, and results vary run to run
Says where time goes, not why: an O(n^2) loop and a legitimately heavy function look the same
CPU profiles are blind to waiting; wall-clock profiles are noisier and need thread filtering (idle threads dominate)
Needs symbols, unwinding info and sometimes runtime flags; inlining and JIT complicate attribution
Flame graphs are easy to misread (the x axis is not time)
whenToUse: A CPU spike or a handler that got slower and the cause is not obvious from metrics and traces
Capacity work: find the top few functions worth optimizing before buying more machines
Comparing two releases, builds or configs with a differential profile
Memory growth or GC pressure: allocation and heap profiles
Always-on continuous profiling for services where regressions are costly
whenNotToUse: The time is spent in other services or the network: use distributed tracing first
The code runs for a few milliseconds per hour: there are too few samples to mean anything
You need exact call counts or exact durations of one call: use an instrumenting profiler or a benchmark
A micro-optimization question on one function: a benchmark with statistics is more precise than a profile
pitfalls: Reading the x axis as time: left to right is alphabetical, and width is share of samples, not chronology
Confusing self and total: a wide box with a thin top edge is a caller, the real cost is in its callees
Sampling a CPU profile of a service that is slow because it waits (locks, database, IO): the profile looks healthy and flat
Too few samples: 100 Hz for 10 seconds is 1,000 samples, and a 3% function gets about 30 of them, plus or minus 10 at 95% confidence
Safepoint bias on the JVM and other runtimes that only sample at safe points, which attributes time to the wrong frame
Missing inline frames: the optimizer folded the hot helper into its caller, so the caller looks guilty
Profiling a debug or differently flagged build, so the profile does not match production
Comparing two flame graphs of different total width: normalize or compare absolute per-request time

roles.label: Service process
roles.description: The running program whose stacks are sampled.

roles.label: Sampler
roles.description: The profiler: a timer or hardware counter that captures stacks at a fixed rate.

roles.label: Profile store
roles.description: Aggregates collapsed stacks per service and version.

roles.label: Flame graph
roles.description: Renders the merged call tree so widths show the share of samples.

quiz.question: In a production flame graph, handle_request is 95% wide with a thin exposed top edge. Directly above it, json_encode is 62% wide, and on top of that encode_loop is 58% wide with a flat top. A tall 12-frame tower at the far left is only 4% wide. Where should you start?
options: At encode_loop, because its wide flat top is where the time is spent
At handle_request, because it is the widest frame and covers almost every sample
At the tall tower on the left, because deep call stacks are slow
At the leftmost frame, because it runs first and delays the rest
quiz.explanation: Self time is the exposed top edge, and encode_loop has nearly all of it. A wide box with a thin top is a caller whose cost sits in its callees. Height is only nesting depth, and left to right is alphabetical, not chronological.

quiz.question: A service shows p99 latency of 2 seconds while CPU sits at 15%. A 100 Hz CPU profile looks flat, with no function above 3%. What should you do next?
options: Raise the CPU sampling rate to 1,000 Hz to find the hidden hot function
Switch to an instrumenting profiler that records every call and return
Treat the flat profile as proof that the code is fine and add more machines for headroom
Take a wall-clock profile to see where threads wait on locks, sockets or disk
quiz.explanation: A CPU profile samples only running threads, so time spent waiting never appears. A wall-clock profile also samples blocked threads and shows the waiting frames. A higher rate or call tracing still sees only running code or adds heavy overhead.

quiz.question: A team profiles at 100 Hz for 10 seconds before and after a release, giving 1,000 samples each. A parser function has 20 samples before and 30 after. They conclude the release made it 50% slower. Is that safe to conclude?
options: Yes, a differential flame graph is exact, so any shift in share is a real change
No, a 10-sample gap at this size is within noise, so profile for much longer
Yes, a 50% relative change is far larger than any plausible error
No, sampling profilers cannot measure functions below 5% of the total
quiz.explanation: At about 3% of 1,000 samples the standard error is roughly 0.5 percentage points on each side, so 2% against 3% could easily be noise. Longer or continuous profiling gives enough samples to tell. Small functions can be measured given enough samples.
